title: ShadowFPT: Backdooring Federated Prompt Tuning via Shadow Triggers

Title:ShadowFPT: Backdooring Federated Prompt Tuning via Shadow Triggers
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Federated Prompt Tuning (FPT) adapts large vision--language models by freezing the pretrained backbone and optimizing only lightweight prompt parameters across clients. Although this design improves communication and parameter efficiency, it creates an overlooked security risk. Since the backbone is shared and frozen, a malicious client can induce backdoor behavior through the representation space while keeping its uploaded prompt updates close to benign ones. We propose \textbf{ShadowFPT}, a targeted backdoor attack that exploits this frozen-backbone attack surface. ShadowFPT first pretrains a learnable \emph{Shadow Trigger} against the frozen CLIP visual encoder, using either auxiliary public data or the malicious client's local data, so that triggered inputs are steered toward the target class in representation space. During federated prompt tuning, the malicious client adapts the trigger under the current global prompt and then optimizes its local prompt on both clean and triggered samples. Only prompt parameters are uploaded to the server, while the trigger and frozen encoders remain local. By shifting most of the attack burden from prompt updates to trigger-induced representation steering, ShadowFPT achieves targeted misclassification while preserving prompt-space stealthiness. Across multiple datasets, aggregation rules, and non-IID federated partitions, ShadowFPT increases the attack success rate from 19.81\% to 90.36\% in our main setting, while maintaining clean accuracy. It remains effective across textual, visual, and joint vision--language prompt tuning. These results identify frozen backbones as stealthy and underexplored backdoor surfaces in federated prompt tuning, suggesting that defenses based only on prompt-update anomaly detection are insufficient.

report.summary: Researchers demonstrate ShadowFPT, a backdoor attack that exploits frozen vision-language backbones in federated prompt tuning, raising attack success from 19.81% to 90.36% while preserving clean accuracy.
report.background: Federated learning lets multiple clients train collaboratively without sharing raw data, and federated prompt tuning (FPT) has become an efficient way to adapt large vision-language models such as CLIP. In FPT, the pretrained backbone stays frozen and clients optimize only lightweight prompt parameters, reducing communication and compute costs. Most security attention has focused on whether uploaded prompt updates look anomalous. But because every client shares the same frozen backbone, the representation space itself can be manipulated. A malicious client can learn a trigger that steers triggered inputs toward a target class while keeping its prompt updates similar to benign ones. This is especially relevant as organizations adopt federated customization for privacy-sensitive vision-language applications and rely on aggregation rules and non-IID data partitions.
key_points: ShadowFPT pretrains a learnable shadow trigger against the frozen CLIP visual encoder using public auxiliary data or the attacker's local data. During federated prompt tuning, the attacker adapts the trigger to the current global prompt and trains its local prompt on both clean and triggered samples. Only prompt parameters are uploaded; the trigger and encoders stay local.

The attack shifts most of the backdoor burden from prompt updates to representation steering. Because malicious prompt updates remain close to benign ones, defenses that only inspect prompt-space anomalies are likely to miss the attack. The trigger itself never leaves the malicious client, making detection harder.

In the main setting, ShadowFPT raises targeted attack success from 19.81% to 90.36% while maintaining clean accuracy. It remains effective across multiple datasets, aggregation rules, non-IID federated partitions, and textual, visual, and joint vision-language prompt tuning.

The paper identifies frozen backbones as a stealthy and underexplored backdoor surface in federated prompt tuning. It argues that security must consider representation-level manipulation, not just anomalous prompt updates, and that existing FPT defenses may be insufficient against trigger-based attacks.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result challenges the assumption that federated prompt tuning is inherently safer because it shares few parameters. Frozen foundation-model backbones become a shared attack surface, so federated vision-language platforms need representation-level backdoor testing, trigger inversion, robust aggregation, and client auditing. Developers building FPT systems should add clean-accuracy plus attack-success evaluations, monitor representation drift, and avoid treating prompt-only anomaly detection as sufficient. Regular users may face targeted misclassification in collaborative vision-language services, though this is a research demonstration rather than an active exploit. The broader lesson is that efficiency-focused adaptation methods can create security blind spots that must be designed for before deployment.
report.tools: To follow up, watch federated learning frameworks such as Flower and FedML for reproducing FPT setups; OpenPrompt and CoOp for prompt-tuning baselines; CLIP as the frozen vision-language backbone; and backdoor detection tools such as Neural Cleanse, STRIP, and ABS for trigger and anomaly checks. Check the paper's arXiv page for code release and compare with robust aggregation methods such as FedAvg variants, Krum, and trimmed mean.
